title: Home Battery Backup Budget Planner
subtitle: Turn an outage wish list into a provider-ready brief and a complete quote comparison.
outcome: Prepare a selected-load outage brief, an evidence-based list of provider questions, two clearly labeled runtime scenarios and a matched all-in budget. Leave technical sizing and installation approval to qualified local professionals.
intro: For U.S. homeowners comparing stationary home-battery proposals for outage backup. This book is not an electrical design, installation manual, emergency plan, medical-device power assessment or a guarantee of continuous service. Use qualified professionals and the equipment maker's requirements for the actual home.

Read the twelve modules on pages 3-14. Pages 15-16 show two completed hypothetical records using the same five prompts as the blank worksheets. Use the seven reusable sheets on pages 17-23. Provider questions, source boundaries and the final review are on pages 24-26.

Original first edition, October 28, 2026. Personal use includes printing the worksheets and sharing your completed records with your own providers and advisers. Please do not redistribute or resell the blank book. The purchase is £9.99 GBP. Project dollar examples are invented USD, not local price benchmarks.

Interactive fields do not calculate automatically. Use a compatible PDF reader, save a copy, then close and reopen it to check entries. The PDF does not upload your information. Completed demonstrations contain invented data, not customer results. Purchase demand and reader usefulness have not been validated.

sections.title: Choose the outage decision you need answered
paras: Write what the household needs during an outage before asking how many batteries to buy. Name the services, desired duration, time of year and activities that can be deferred. 'Keep the entire home normal' and 'keep selected communication and refrigeration loads available overnight' are different briefs. Do not let a broad sales label define your needs for you.

Record existing solar, planned equipment, occupancy and any use that requires a separate professional contingency plan. A device essential to health or safety needs advice from its appropriate provider; a generic battery calculation is not evidence that it will operate continuously. Keep that requirement visibly outside an unverified household runtime exercise.

Ask the installer whether the proposal supplies partial-home or whole-home backup and exactly which circuits or equipment are covered. Tesla's manufacturer-specific backup guide distinguishes these arrangements and says the final design depends on the home [Tesla backup]. Its statements about one product do not establish the capabilities of another brand.

Finish the brief with one decision: compare two proposals against the same selected loads and duration, or establish what additional assessment is needed. The useful output may be a list of missing evidence. A completed owner worksheet does not authorize installation, connection or operation of equipment.

sections.title: Keep power, energy and starting demand distinct
paras: Power describes the rate at which energy is delivered; energy describes an amount delivered over time. Keep watts or kilowatts separate from watt-hours or kilowatt-hours. DOE's March 11, 2019 storage explainer illustrates that output capability and storage duration are separate dimensions [DOE]. This dated source is used for terminology, not today's equipment costs or demand.

For an arithmetic check, average watts multiplied by operating hours and divided by 1,000 gives kWh. Average consumption is not the same thing as an appliance's startup demand or maximum operating power. Do not add average watts and treat the sum as an approved inverter or circuit rating.

Ask the provider to identify continuous output, temporary or starting-load capability, applicable duration and any simultaneous-load limits in the actual configuration. More stored energy does not automatically increase the inverter's output. Record the evidence for any promised combination of appliances rather than judging compatibility from the battery's kWh label.

The CARB residential backup tool explicitly distinguishes power and energy needs and warns that its generic assumptions do not determine a particular home's demand [CARB]. This planner follows the same boundary. Its calculations help check stated inputs; technical sizing, protection, site suitability and installation remain professional responsibilities.

sections.title: Case 1: build a transparent energy list
paras: Invented selected-load exercise, with assumed average consumption only: refrigeration averages 120 W for 12 hours; router 15 W for 12 hours; selected lights 40 W for 5 hours; laptop 60 W for 3 hours. These are fictional inputs for arithmetic, not typical ratings, recommendations or measurements from a real home.

Refrigeration: 120 x 12 / 1,000 = 1.44 kWh. Router: 15 x 12 / 1,000 = 0.18 kWh. Lights: 40 x 5 / 1,000 = 0.20 kWh. Laptop: 60 x 3 / 1,000 = 0.18 kWh. Total energy over the listed operating periods is 2.00 kWh.

Adding the four listed average rates gives 235 W, but those averages do not establish the maximum simultaneous demand or any motor-start requirement. The 2.00 kWh sum also does not prove that a 2 kWh advertised battery would deliver the requested service. Available starting energy, conversion, controls, power limits and actual duty cycles remain unresolved.

Give this record to the provider with the source of each input and ask what is missing. For a cycling appliance, identify whether the value is an average over a measured interval or an instantaneous rating. Obtain appropriate professional evidence rather than opening equipment or attempting electrical measurements outside your competence.

sections.title: Establish the usable energy basis once
paras: Ask whether the quoted kWh figure is nominal battery capacity, usable stored energy, or energy available to AC loads under stated conditions. Record the boundary exactly. If the provider already gives an AC-available amount that includes conversion and operating limits, do not apply the same reductions a second time.

Record the assumed energy at the instant the outage begins. A system advertised with a full-charge capacity may not be full at that moment. Ask how normal operation, the chosen control strategy and site conditions affect that assumption. This is a question for the provider's scenario, not an instruction to change a setting.

Distinguish a backup reserve from a protected shutdown floor. Tesla's Backup Reserve guide says its reserved energy becomes available during an outage [Tesla reserve]. Therefore it would be wrong to subtract that reserve automatically as though it were inaccessible outage energy. Other products and configurations need their own documentation.

Write an energy bridge with a named basis for every adjustment. If a loss factor or lower operating limit is unknown, mark it unknown. Do not use a convenient percentage as a universal engineering allowance. Ask the qualified provider for both the explanation and the conditions under which the figure is expected to hold.

sections.title: Case 2: check a conditional runtime quotient
paras: Invented model: a 14 kWh usable stored-energy basis is at 75% state of charge at outage start, giving 10.5 kWh before the next stated adjustment. A fictional provider supplies a single combined 80% factor for the available energy delivered to AC loads under the scenario. This factor includes the model's conversion and operating-floor treatment; it is not a generic efficiency recommendation.

Available AC energy = 14 x 0.75 x 0.80 = 8.40 kWh. With a constant 0.70 kW AC load, no recharge and the assumed compatible power capability, the quotient is 8.40 / 0.70 = 12 hours. At 1.40 kW under otherwise identical assumptions, it is 6 hours.

Neither quotient promises actual outage duration. They ignore changing appliance use, temperature effects beyond the supplied factor, starting events and interruptions. Check the power constraint independently: for example, a hypothetical 5 kW continuous rating alone does not prove support for an unresolved 7 kW starting event. Ask for the relevant temporary rating, duration and equipment compatibility.

Do not subtract an app's backup reserve again from the 8.40 kWh figure. Confirm whether that reserve is available in the outage and whether any protected minimum was already included. Keep a provider-confirmed AC figure separate from an owner arithmetic illustration. A lower start-of-outage charge can change the result even when the installed equipment is identical.

sections.title: Describe what happens while the grid is absent
paras: Ask which functions continue when the grid is down: which loads are supplied, whether existing solar can operate and recharge the battery in that configuration, and which operating conditions must be met. Ownership of solar panels or a battery does not by itself document the complete backup capability of the proposed system.

Keep the physical equipment list beside the functional promise. Record controllers, isolation or transfer equipment as items for the installer to identify and price. Ask for compatibility confirmation for the existing solar equipment and the proposed system. The owner brief does not supply a wiring arrangement, switching procedure or commissioning method.

Use a no-recharge scenario as one explicit comparison, then a separately supported low-recharge scenario where relevant. CARB notes that solar contribution depends on weather, season, angle and shading [CARB]. A projected annual solar total is not proof that energy will arrive during the particular outage window you care about.

Ask how the provider's model handles time of day, power capability, recharging limits and periods when the battery cannot deliver service. Daily energy accounting can reveal a shortage but does not resolve the timing within a day. For commissioning and operation, rely on qualified providers and manufacturer instructions, not a spreadsheet test.

sections.title: Case 3: reveal a second-day shortfall
paras: Invented two-period energy ledger: start period 1 with 8.0 kWh available to the selected AC loads. The loads need 6.0 kWh in each period. Assume 1.5 kWh of additional AC-equivalent usable recharge arrives after each period's load draw. Ignore other losses because the energy boundary is already AC-available. The maximum available-energy capacity is 8.0 kWh.

After period 1's draw, 8.0 - 6.0 = 2.0 kWh remains; then recharge raises the next starting amount to 3.5 kWh. During period 2, only 3.5 kWh is available before the assumed late recharge, so the 6.0 kWh requirement has a 2.5 kWh timing shortfall. The later 1.5 kWh cannot serve an earlier unmet load.

If someone instead pools the entire second period's energy, 3.5 + 1.5 = 5.0 kWh still falls 1.0 kWh below the 6.0 kWh requirement. That aggregate deficit is smaller than the 2.5 kWh pre-recharge gap because it ignores when the energy arrives. Both calculations are consistent but answer different questions.

Do not write a negative ending battery charge as if the system could deliver it. Record unserved energy or a gap instead. This scenario demonstrates why 'recharges every day' is incomplete. It does not establish how an actual system would behave, which loads would stop, or a safe household contingency plan.

sections.title: Price the complete installed boundary
paras: Request an itemized scope that identifies the battery, conversion equipment, backup controls, installation, assessment, permit and utility-related tasks, supporting electrical work, access, restoration and any monitoring or service charges. Some may be bundled, some separate, and some not required. Unknown inclusions should not become zero-cost assumptions.

Separate existing-home work from the battery package. A provider may need to assess service equipment, space, structural support or compatibility. Ask who assesses each issue, who obtains applicable approvals and whether the quote is fixed or provisional. This planner does not determine the applicable code, placement, clearance or installation requirements.

Use the same backup brief for all proposals. A lower price for fewer covered loads is an alternative scope, not a direct saving on equivalent service. Retain the quoted total and the matched-scope analysis in separate columns. Ask for a revised written proposal before treating an owner's adjustment as a real offer.

Record purchase, lease, loan or service obligations according to the actual agreement, but do not let a small starting payment replace the full installed-cost record. Keep the gross project cost separate from unverified incentives or future bill savings. This book supplies neither a national battery-price range nor personal financing advice.

sections.title: Case 4: normalize the missing scope
paras: Invented USD proposals for the same selected-load brief: A's headline is $11,800. It excludes a separately priced $1,800 backup-control package, $1,200 supporting-work allowance and $500 application/permit package. B quotes $14,900 including the matched controls, applications and the same $1,200 supporting-work allowance. Assume equipment and all other scope are equivalent for this demonstration.

A's analysis total = $11,800 + $1,800 + $1,200 + $500 = $15,300. B remains $14,900. The matched-scope difference is $400 in B's favor. Comparing only headlines would have suggested a $3,100 advantage for A, but the scopes were different.

If the provider-confirmed supporting work later becomes $2,000 instead of the $1,200 allowance for both, add the $800 difference once. A becomes $16,100 and B becomes $15,700. The $400 comparison difference remains, while the household commitment scenario increases for both. Neither analysis is a contractor's revised offer until confirmed in writing.

For a separate owner planning ceiling of $17,000, the second scenario leaves $900 of headroom for A and $1,300 for B before any other owner costs. Headroom is not a recommendation for a contingency percentage or proof that all costs are covered. Ask which uncertainty remains and keep alternative scopes separate.

sections.title: Record limits that a warranty label hides
paras: Ask for the exact warranty document and responsible entity for the equipment, installation workmanship and ongoing service. Record term, retained-capacity conditions, throughput or usage limits if specified, labor and access exclusions, claim steps and transfer terms. The word 'warranty' alone does not define the owner's future obligation.

Clarify whether a promised duration refers to warranty coverage, expected product life, a modeled outage runtime or a service response. These are different claims. A capacity-retention provision does not promise that every appliance will run for a particular number of hours years from now.

Record who monitors system status, what information is available without an internet connection, who responds to a fault and what documentation the owner receives at handover. Ask what happens if the original installer stops providing service. Do not assume that remote monitoring is the same as a staffed emergency response.

Have the provider explain applicable location, approvals, compatibility and safety responsibilities using current manufacturer instructions and local requirements. The workbook intentionally gives no installation clearances, connection steps, fire-response procedure or equipment troubleshooting. It is a place to record qualified answers and the documents supporting them.

sections.title: Use the two completed records as a guide
paras: The next two demonstration pages fill the same five prompts used in Worksheet 1 and Worksheet 6. They connect the fictional selected-load case to the fictional quote comparison. They are not a customer testimonial, a real installer assessment or an endorsement of a battery model.

Notice how unknowns remain visible: no approved starting-load assessment, no verified outage recharge, and provisional supporting work. A useful completed record does not make every cell look settled. It identifies the next question, responsible provider and evidence required before reliance.

For your own packet, keep the raw evidence in attachments with dates. Summarize only the facts needed for this decision in the worksheet. An input from a bill, a provider measurement, a technical report and an owner's preference should be labeled differently rather than all appearing as verified measurements.

Share a completed copy with your chosen professional if useful, after removing unrelated personal information. Keep a blank master. Saving or forwarding a worksheet does not amend an installation agreement. Retain the provider's accepted final scope and its stated assumptions separately.

sections.title: Decide what needs clarification before purchase
paras: Check essential gaps before ranking proposals: missing selected-load coverage, unclear usable-energy boundary, unsupported starting capability, assumed recharge or omitted supporting work. A low total or an attractive hours claim does not resolve those gaps. A request for further assessment can be the correct next decision.

Make a short list of the assumptions that most change the comparison. Examples here include start-of-outage charge, average load, arrival time of recharge and final supporting-work cost. Ask the provider to explain alternatives against the same brief. Do not choose the most optimistic assumption as the only base case.

Write a decision memo naming the current proposal revision, remaining questions, who must answer them and what would change your choice. Confirm scope, payment terms, handover and applicable approvals with qualified parties. This workbook does not select equipment or authorize a transaction on your behalf.

The Solar Quote Comparison Workbook covers generation offers, ownership and bill assumptions. General HomeCostEngine energy guides cover broader upgrades. This title focuses on outage-service boundaries, starting energy, conditional duration, recharge timing and battery quote scope. Those concepts are related, but the cases, records and substantive wording here are newly authored.

questions: Which selected loads and circuits are actually covered during an outage?
What evidence supports their average, simultaneous and starting requirements?
Does the energy figure mean nominal storage, usable storage or AC-available energy?
What charge at outage start does the duration illustration assume?
Which adjustments already include conversion or protected operating limits?
Is a stated backup reserve available during the outage for this product?
Can the proposed solar/battery configuration recharge while the grid is absent?
How does the model handle recharge timing, poor weather and a second day?
Which controls, applications and supporting-work costs are included or provisional?
Who confirms site suitability, applicable approvals and equipment compatibility?
What do warranties cover, and who pays for service, labor or access?
Which written revision and qualified answers close the remaining decision gaps?

No organization endorses this book.
overlap: Existing solar and energy titles discuss broader offers, consumption and scope. This title's distinct output is an outage brief joined to available-energy, power, recharge-timing and complete battery-quote records. No substantive passage or worked case is copied. Document layout and the established delivery code are reused. The free article gives a checklist and one duration illustration; the paid book adds all four cases, seven reusable sheets and two completed demonstrations.
final_checks: Can another person identify the exact outage services requested and distinguish preferences from verified technical evidence?
Are W, kW and kWh labeled, with average consumption separated from simultaneous and starting demand?
Does each energy adjustment have a stated boundary, without counting losses twice or treating an available backup reserve as inaccessible?
Do duration illustrations state starting charge, AC-available energy, load, recharge timing and limits? They are not a guarantee of service.
Does the matched quote include the appropriate controls and supporting work, with provisional costs kept visible?
Are qualified assessment, approvals, warranty and service responsibilities recorded with supporting documents?
